user_policy.application: Sliver framework implementation is hostile, including operator-side C2 transport. Mere references and generic library mechanics do not establish the implementation fingerprint.

scope: Second static behavior review of the ten samples initially placed in purgatory.
methods: Read complete source and collected cleave facts for all ten.
Decoded gzip/Base64 artwork without executing it.
Reconstructed and statically disassembled the existing WinExec stub with a sentinel function address.
Traced source-to-sink behavior, inputs, entry points, and missing dependencies.
Fetched the public OffensiveGolang source archive, verified the example content hash, and inspected the called helper implementations.
Parsed the embedded bot public key using OpenSSL; did not contact sample destinations.
limits: This is static source analysis, not an endpoint detonation or a forensic examination of a real host.
Missing dependencies and missing endpoint context are called out per case; this does not claim complete reverse engineering of every surrounding program.

samples.artifact_role: Standalone Go staging-shaped example with an inert embedded payload
confirmed_behavior: Main decodes a constant Base64 string and decompresses gzip data.
The decoded object is 1609 bytes of ASCII artwork/filler, SHA-256 6a14b866e012fd643a1239ddb684ba40dce39157b5f2d56d46d6d914c46388cf; no ELF, MZ, or shebang header.
It attempts to write the decoded bytes to /tmp/.x with mode 0755, then invokes that path using os/exec.
samples.interpretation: Investigate the hidden executable staging attempt. The actual embedded content does not establish a functioning malicious payload. On the ordinary Unix Go execution path, os/exec directly starts the file without shell interpretation; this artwork is not a normal executable.
limits: No runtime execution was performed.

Ignored write errors and a predictable /tmp path mean the code does not guarantee that the bytes eventually executed are the bytes decoded here; existing files/symlinks and permissions are endpoint context.
The code performs one gzip Read, not a guaranteed read-to-EOF; all observed decoded bytes are artwork.
samples.disposition_reason: Retain purgatory for an unsafe staging/execution template with inert embedded content; neither a proven hostile payload nor ordinary benign functionality.

confirmed_behavior: Builds a 26-byte x64 stub that reserves stack space, sets the display mode in EDX, loads the resolved WinExec address, calls it, restores RSP, and returns. Static disassembly confirms the instructions.
Pads the stub to offset 32 and appends the command line. The thread parameter points at that command string; the stub preserves the incoming RCX parameter.
Allocates remote RWX memory, writes the payload there, and starts a remote thread at that allocation. The caller supplies the process handle and command.
samples.interpretation: This implements real process injection. An unexplained process performing these operations is a high-priority endpoint finding. Comments about winlogon/SYSTEM are intended-use context, not evidence that this file acquires such a handle or crosses a privilege boundary.
limits: No callers, process-handle acquisition, target process identity, or actual injected command are included.
The existing code was only disassembled; no injection or sample execution occurred.
samples.disposition_reason: Retain purgatory as an offensive injection primitive with actual mechanics, but without an established unauthorized target or end-to-end payload in the supplied artifact.

confirmed_behavior: Uses Sliver client configuration and SliverRPCClient types, and implements the framework-specific WireGuard connection and configuration functions.
Constructs/configures a WireGuard device from supplied client/server keys and endpoint configuration, calls dev.Up, and routes gRPC dialing through the tunnel.
Obtains mTLS dial options, dials the RPC client, caches idle tunnels, and retries deadline failures within a bounded window.
samples.interpretation: This is Sliver framework operational transport code, rather than a generic vendored library or an implant dispatcher. Under the user policy, Sliver itself is hostile; operator-side authentication and lack of an implant dispatcher do not make this artifact benign.
limits: Does not prove that the transport ran on any endpoint or that a particular server was contacted.
No claim that this source file implements implant task dispatch.
samples.disposition_reason: Move from purgatory to bad under the explicit Sliver-hostile instruction. Require both a content-derived framework implementation fingerprint and a concrete Sliver RPC/WireGuard channel finding.

samples.artifact_role: Offline private-scalar recovery and signature-forgery exploit helpers
confirmed_behavior: Derives the nonce prefix from the fixed Tor domain string alone, with no secret prefix.
RecoverBlindedScalar computes (S-r) times the modular inverse of the signature challenge modulo the group order.
UnblindScalar removes the blinding multiplier; ForgeBlindedSignature constructs a signature from a supplied recovered scalar.
samples.interpretation: These are real attacker-side cryptographic recovery/forgery operations for a specific vulnerable signing construction. The educational header does not erase the capability. The file does not locate a victim service or acquire a signature by itself.
limits: Curve helpers and a vulnerable target signing implementation are outside the supplied file.
No real key was recovered and no signature forgery was executed; the assessment follows the data flow and algebra.
samples.disposition_reason: Retain purgatory as specialized exploitation tooling with an educational context and missing target/input acquisition, rather than declaring it harmless from its header.

samples.artifact_role: TSPkg password recovery from a virtual-address reader
confirmed_behavior: Locates and walks TSPkg credential structures using a supplied module, template, and virtual-address reader.
Reads the primary credential structure, username/domain UNICODE_STRING fields, and password ciphertext through r.ReadVA.
Calls decryptLSA with a caller-supplied LSA key, decodes the result as UTF-16, and returns credentials indexed by logon-session LUID; String can render Domain/User:Password.
samples.interpretation: This is credential extraction, not mere credential-related vocabulary. An unexplained live LSASS reader invoking this path would be a serious credential-access finding. The reader abstraction alone does not tell whether the input is live memory or a forensic dump.
limits: The reader implementation, memory acquisition, LSA key acquisition, and callers are absent.
Setting a Go password string field to empty does not prove secure erasure of every copy.
samples.disposition_reason: Retain purgatory: real password-recovery capability, with the live-versus-offline acquisition and authorization context unresolved.

samples.interpretation: The hostname and beacon path warrant investigation, but neither spelling proves controller ownership, vendor affiliation, or a tasking protocol. This is a phone-home/network indicator, not a demonstrated remote command channel.

samples.artifact_role: Upstream OffensiveGolang evasive injection example with placeholder inputs
confirmed_behavior: The artifact SHA-256 exactly matches examples/c2/earlyInjection_pe/earlyInjection_pe.go in the fetched upstream archive at commit afa9edfc51a3b256bf8c81092bbc26eb9674026c.

At that upstream revision, CheckNameEXE exits unless the executable basename matches main.exe; CheckMouse samples mouse movement five seconds apart and exits if stationary; CheckScreen exits for a sufficiently small display.

The matched upstream injector decodes Base64 inputs and constructs AES-CTR before creating a suspended target. The literal placeholder key in this artifact starts with an invalid Base64 character, yields no valid AES key, and cannot pass the subsequent key slice/cipher setup.
The upstream helper contains section-based injection and thread-context redirection code, but these placeholder inputs fail before its process-creation step.
samples.interpretation: An evasive injection template is a high-interest endpoint artifact even when its payload has not been populated. The supplied example is incomplete, and its current constants are not a usable injected payload.
limits: The sample supplies no go.mod/go.sum pinning its dependency revision. The failure analysis is explicitly for the inspected upstream revision, not every possible replacement of that import.
No source or downloaded helper was compiled or executed.
samples.disposition_reason: Retain purgatory as an incomplete offensive injection example with confirmed anti-analysis gates, rather than labeling it benign because the payload is a placeholder.

confirmed_behavior: Accepts Stage1Bytes and PayloadBlob from its caller and emits an x86-64 ET_DYN ELF with two page-aligned PT_LOAD segments.
Sets the first segment read/execute, the second read-only, and the entry point to the first segment. Omits section headers, PT_INTERP, and PT_DYNAMIC.
Copies the supplied bytes into the output buffer and returns it. The file performs no filesystem write, subprocess launch, network transfer, encryption, or decryption.
samples.interpretation: The source is an executable-image builder intended to carry stages/payloads. Sectionlessness and ET_DYN alone do not prove malware or evasion. The actual stage bytes and the caller that deploys/runs the result determine its operational meaning.
limits: No stage-one machine code, payload blob, or deployment/execution caller is supplied.
Prior packer wording must not be read as evidence that this function itself encrypts, compresses, or executes anything.
samples.disposition_reason: Retain purgatory as an unexplained staged-payload carrier builder; do not assign hostile execution or encryption claims to its generic serialization operations.

samples.artifact_role: Keyed bot bootstrap with a fixed hub and disguised transport configuration
confirmed_behavior: Decodes an embedded 294-byte DER public key; OpenSSL parses it as RSA-2048 with exponent 65537.
Creates a base.NewClientM client, assigns the hub public key, registers a CPU-information initializer, and starts it against cs8425.noip.me:8787.
With the source constants enabled, installs a fake-HTTP TLS dialer with browser-like cookies/User-Agent and WebSocket mode. Sets AutoClean true and Daemon false.
samples.interpretation: A fixed keyed hub combined with disguised bot transport is a strong C2 lead. The AIS3 TEST BOT label is attacker-controlled context, not an authorization proof. This deserves a higher investigative priority than a generic network library.
limits: Implementations of local/base, lib/fakehttp, and local/toolkit were not present in the supplied local Go cohorts and were not resolved upstream.
AutoClean is a configuration flag; its actual cleanup effect is unknown. The third boolean passed to NewTLSClient is also uninterpreted without that implementation.
No command dispatcher, persistence implementation, or actual host execution was established; the hub was not contacted.
samples.disposition_reason: Retain purgatory for a highly suspicious C2 bootstrap with unresolved core protocol/command implementation, not because a test label makes it trustworthy.

confirmed_behavior: exfiltrate joins the entire os.Environ result into one string and places that value in the env form field of http.PostForm.
The target URL is supplied by the caller. There is no filtering/redaction, local-only restriction, consent mechanism, or calling entry point in the supplied file.
samples.interpretation: If invoked against an external unauthorized recipient, this is environment exfiltration and can disclose credentials. The source-to-request relationship is established; actual invocation, recipient, and environment contents are not. A diagnostic/authorized exporter remains possible from this isolated function.
limits: No caller, destination value, endpoint execution, or actual secret contents were supplied.

One versus two hostile trait directories is a coverage gate, not a reason to decide whether the behavior is malicious. The prior rationale incorrectly mixed that gate into the disposition explanation.
samples.disposition_reason: Retain purgatory because recipient and invocation context are unresolved while full-environment export is too risky for benign training; this decision is independent of trait counts.
samples.prior_rationale: Posts the complete process environment to a caller-supplied URL. A synthetic exfiltration positive control, with unknown runtime destination and reachability. Existing scanner emits one hostile directory; retain in purgatory rather than inventing a second independent hostile finding.
